title: The CEO’s Dilemma: You Can’t Be in Every Room
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell addresses a basic scaling problem for chief executives: once a company reaches hundreds of people, the important decisions about customers, features, hiring, and spending are made constantly by people several layers removed from the CEO. He grounds the problem in Helmuth von Moltke's Auftragstaktik, in which commanders made objectives and intent clear and trained officers to act on that understanding as conditions changed. Revisiting his earlier argument that a good management system turns managers into extensions of CEO intent, he proposes that AI can now extend that intent further by giving every employee access to a model that knows the mission, values, strategic objectives, and how the CEO balances stakeholder tradeoffs. Two examples, a remote salesperson weighing a discount request and a software team deciding whether to pause its roadmap for a quality issue, show the AI supplying organizational context while employees supply local facts. Trammell insists the AI must be a thinking partner rather than an oracle, that the CEO must still communicate constantly, and that the tool complements rather than replaces the management system.
points: Trammell frames AI's highest-leverage enterprise use not as a fancy search engine but as a 24/7 version of commander's intent available to every employee at the moment of decision.
Auftragstaktik worked because the Prussian army invested in doctrine and training so officers understood the larger purpose and could act without waiting for instructions.
An intent-aware AI can tell a salesperson that margin protection is a current priority and the company competes on service rather than price, while the rep still decides how to handle the customer.
Employees closest to a situation hold information neither the CEO nor the AI can see, so the model should contribute context about objectives, values, and stakeholder tradeoffs rather than answers.
The approach only works if the CEO keeps explaining mission, priorities, and tradeoffs, because AI can reinforce and distribute intent but cannot substitute for clear communication.
quotes: When a company is small, the CEO can make or directly shape most of the important calls: which customers to pursue, which features to build, which people to hire, where to spend, what to prioritize. At 500 people, those decisions are being made all day, every day, throughout the organization, often by people several layers removed from the CEO.

A commander made the objective and his intent clear, then relied on subordinates to use their judgment as conditions changed. The Prussian army spent a lot of time building that mechanism with doctrine and training designed to help officers understand the larger purpose and act without waiting for instructions.

Imagine giving every employee access to an AI that understands how the CEO wants the company to operate. It knows the long-term mission and vision. It knows the values that differentiate the organization and how those values guide tradeoffs.

The AI can surface that reducing enterprise churn is a strategic objective and that reliability is one of the company’s differentiating values. The team still brings the facts the AI cannot see: the severity of the bug, the technical risk and what customers are telling them.

The AI should be a thinking partner, not an oracle. Employees closest to a situation will usually have information that the CEO and the AI do not. Their judgment about the customer, people, technical constraints and immediate circumstances remains essential.
This complements the management system rather than replacing it. Managers still translate strategy, coach employees and exercise judgment. Employees still respond to the facts in front of them.
